en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui, Part Two:
Distinguishing the Various Sages, Section Four: One, The Gate of Awakening Revealed through Objects, Subsection Six: One, The Object of Form (*rūpa*).
“If form-conception forms dust, and one’s refined discernment cannot penetrate through it, how can one fail to achieve clear penetration and thereby attain perfect interfusion?
Upānanda, by contemplating the impurities of white bones and subtle dust, analyzed form to clarify emptiness; once the dust of form was exhausted, the wondrous form became subtle and perfectly round.
Now, this selection states:

"Form is bound by false conceptualization, which defiles the true nature; its substance is inherently coarse and its essence is obstructive, lacking clarity and penetration. How can one take this non-penetrating dharma as the means to attain perfect penetration?"
2. The Object of Sound.
"Sound is mixed with language; it consists merely of phonemes, phrases, and meanings. Since one does not contain all others, how can one attain perfect penetration?"
"Kaundinya realized the Four Truths because the sound of the wondrous voice was subtle and perfect; thus he attained the Way.
Now, this selection clarifies that sound does not depart from various mixed languages, and language is nothing other than names, phrases, and syllables.
Names and phrases each have their own distinct limits: names express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while phrases express specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*).
Syllables (*vyañjana*) are identical to letters (*akṣara*); as the basis for both [names and phrases], they cannot by themselves alone contain everything.
"Yi" means "this. Third, the realm of fragrance:
"Fragrance is known through contact; when separated, it is fundamentally non-existent. Since its perception is not constant, how can one attain perfect penetration?"

The youth Gandhahastin was dwelling in quiet seclusion within a pure chamber; when the fragrance reached his nose, he contemplated this state of non-arising, seeing that it came from nowhere and went nowhere.
Once the dust-like vapors have been extinguished, the wondrous fragrance becomes subtle and pervasive.
Now, this text discriminates:
if the single dharma of fragrance were to exist when conjoined and cease to exist when separated, it would not be constant; therefore, it does not yet constitute a perfect contemplation.
4. The Object of Taste.
"The nature of taste is not original; it exists only when there is tasting. Since its perception is not constant or uniform, how can one attain perfect penetration?"
Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, by tasting various flavors and realizing that flavor is without arising— neither identical to body and mind nor separate from body and mind—
attained the stage of Bodhisattva through the clarity of their awareness of flavor.
Now it is said:

"The nature of taste is fundamentally non-existent; it is only perceived in dependence upon the sense organ. Without the organ, there is no taste; therefore, this is not the path of universal penetration.
"At the time of taste" means at the time of tasting.
5. The Realm of Touch.
"Touch is clarified by that which is touched; there is nothing it does not clearly touch. Since its nature of union and separation is not fixed, how can one attain perfect penetration?"

Bhadrapāla suddenly awakened to the cause of water: since it neither washes away dust nor washes the body, it is tranquil in between, attaining a state of non-existence; the sublime touch was proclaimed and clarified, whereby he realized the fruit of enlightenment.

Now it is explained that this contact (sparśa) is manifested by depending on the body that is contacted; there is nothing it does not manifest, yet its nature is not constant or fixed, and therefore it is not perfectly penetrating.
Sixth, the objective field of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
“The dharmas are called internal objects; relying on objects, there must be a subject. Since subject and object do not encompass all things, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Mahākāśyapa, observing that the six external objects of the world are subject to decay and ruin, cultivated the extinction of all things through emptiness and stillness alone. Thus the wondrous Dharma was proclaimed and clarified, extinguishing all outflows (*āsrava*).

Now, although this selection is called the "Wondrous Dharma," it is nonetheless an internal dust; relying on this for cultivation, how could one transcend the duality of subject and object? Since awakening is neither subject nor object, this is not the perfect penetration that universally encompasses and penetrates all.
2. Entering the Gate by Testimony through the Sense Organs (Five Sections): 1. The Eye Organ.
"Although the nature of seeing is transparently clear, it sees what is before but not what is behind; the four quarters are deficient by half. How can this be considered perfect penetration?"
Āniruddha attained realization by cultivating the Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Illumination; he turned his vision back to follow its source, and through this, he achieved his proof.

Now, although what is called "seeing-nature" carries the meaning of being thoroughly clear and illuminating, [the text] states that the front is entirely bright while the back is entirely dark, and when looking to the left and right, only two-thirds are visible; thus it is said that "the four quarters are deficient by one half."
2. The Nose Faculty.

"The inhalation and exhalation of the breath pass through one another; yet, in their present manifestation, there is no mingling of the airs. They remain fragmented and do not interpenetrate; how, then, can perfect penetration be attained?"

"Couli Panthaka, by practicing counting the breaths, reached the subtlest level where he exhausted [the perception of] arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; he then reversed the breath to follow emptiness, and thereby attained the Way.

Now you say that although the breath passes through the nose in both inhalation and exhalation, each movement occupies its own place without intersecting the other; since the parts are thus separated, how can this constitute a complete contemplation?"
3. The Tongue Faculty.
"The tongue is not an entrance without a source; it gives rise to cognition because of flavors. When flavors cease, cognition has no existence; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"

Kauṇḍinya observed that the cognition of taste is neither the substance nor the object; he returned to the taste and turned back upon the cognition, thereby attaining the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*).

However, to say now that the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-āyatana*) does not exist independently of causes, but arises only through the conjunction of the taste-object and the sense-field, such that cognition perishes when the object ceases—this is not yet a comprehensive understanding.
4. The Body Faculty.
"The body and its objects of touch are each distinct from Perfect Enlightenment; their boundaries do not merge. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"
Piliṅgavatsa, by means of contemplating painful sensations, realized a pure mind free from both perception and pain; with his body left behind as pure sensation, he attained the fruit of arhatship.

Now it is said that the perceiving body-faculty and the perceived object of touch exist only in mutual dependence, each lacking intrinsic nature; since these cases are analogous, neither constitutes a perfect contemplation. Because knowing and non-knowing differ and each has its own limits, they do not merge into one another; therefore, they are excluded.
5. The Faculty of Mind.

"The faculty of mind involves scattered thoughts; though it may reach a state of profound clarity, it ultimately lacks true vision. Since its conceptualizations cannot be shed, how can one attain perfect penetration?"

Subhūti had attained unimpeded mind throughout kalpas past; by means of this observation, he perceived the ten directions as empty. As the nature of emptiness became perfectly luminous, he suddenly entered the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-like clarity and emptiness, becoming one with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Now, it is said that the faculty of mind involves confused and discursive thoughts; yet, if one employs the profound rotation of tranquil concentration, ultimately there will be no cognition or vision.
If one practices in reliance upon this, how can conceptual thoughts escape?

Furthermore, if one looks toward the profound awakening of true luminosity, there will necessarily be no cognition or perception; that is, there is no awareness of luminosity. One should know that those who possess cognition and perception have not yet escaped delusive thought.
3. The Section on Cultivating Severance Based on Consciousness (Six Parts):
1. Eye-consciousness:

"Consciousness perceives through a mixture of the three harmonies; when the root is questioned, it is called 'without characteristics. Its own essence has no prior fixed nature; how, then, can it attain perfect penetration?"

Śāriputra’s mind has been pure in its perception for kalpas; yet, because he encountered the Buddha, his vision and awakening became perfectly clear, and his luminosity reached the ultimate limit of knowledge and insight.

Now, [the Buddha] distinguishes that the eye-consciousness is intermingled within the triad of subject, object, and contact. When one exhaustively investigates its fundamental nature, no characteristic can be found; its own essence is not permanent—how, then, could it be perfect and pervasive?
2. Ear-consciousness:
"The mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions through the power of great causal roots; yet the initial mind cannot enter it—how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva fundamentally employs mental hearing to discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings, thereby attaining great mastery.

The present [text] excludes those who are too exalted and fails to encompass all capacities; since the Dharma-realm constitutes his essence and mental hearing constitutes his function, he penetrates the ten directions. This is the result of Samantabhadra’s realization through his cultivation of the Great Practice; therefore, those of middling and inferior capacities are entirely excluded from this, which is why it is said that they "cannot enter."

Because the practitioner who illuminates Samantabhadra within the minds of sentient beings must first manifest his body, this is not the same as Avalokiteśvara, who manifests according to whatever object he encounters.
Third, the nose-consciousness.
"Contemplating the nose is originally a provisional means, intended only to cause the mind to settle. Once settled, the mind finds its abode; how then can one attain perfect penetration?

Sundarananda contemplated the white tip of his nose; he saw the incoming and outgoing breaths transform into radiant light, so that his body and mind were internally illuminated, and the world became perfectly transparent, universally pure and empty.
Now, discerning that contemplating the nose is not the ultimate, it is called a provisional capacity.
If one were to cause the mind to be gathered [in this way], it would necessarily result in a place of dwelling; yet the true source is non-dwelling, so such a dwelling is incorrect.
The Sūtra says: "If the mind has a dwelling place, it is not truly dwelling.
Fourth is the consciousness of the tongue:
"When preaching the Dharma by playing with sounds and characters, one who first attains awakening finds that names and phrases are not outflow-free; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"
Pūrṇa possesses unimpeded eloquence and has attained fearlessness through his subtle and profound elucidation of the secret Dharma-gates.

Now, he selects that the teaching of the Dharma does not depart from sounds, names, phrases, and syllables; those who are to be awakened must first be matured, for one cannot enter the Path without seeds.
If one speaks with a distracted mind, it merely constitutes something outflowing (*sāsrava*) and cannot be called perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).
Fifth, the consciousness of the body:

"Holding precepts and violating them merely constrains the body; yet if there were no body, there would be nothing to constrain. Since this [consciousness] originally does not pervade all things, how can it attain perfect penetration?"

Because Upāli maintained the pure prohibitions, he thereby disciplined his body and attained mastery over it; he then gradually disciplined his mind and achieved thorough penetration of it, whereupon both body and mind became entirely unimpeded.
Now, when examining the subtle conduct of upholding or violating precepts, one inspects only the body; yet if the body does not arise, what is there to be restrained?
Therefore, [the mind] cannot be universally pervasive regarding all phenomena (dharmas).
Sixth, the mental consciousness.

“Supernatural powers are fundamentally rooted in past causes; how could they be related to the discrimination of dharmas? Since mindfulness depends on conditions and is not separate from objects, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Mahāmaudgalyāyana attained great spiritual efficacy because, through the cultivation of meditative concentration, he turned back the turbid consciousness and manifested the light of the mind.

Now, these supernormal powers (abhijñā) are originally present as a result of past causes; they are manifested through the power of applied effort (prayoga). How could they be related to the rules for meditative cultivation, such that consciousness must first arise before they can be attained?
"Dharma" means the sense of a guiding rule or standard.
"Discrimination" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The mental consciousness takes objects as its conditions and discriminates all things; because it does not depart from sensory realms, it is not the path of perfect penetration.
4. The Section on Returning to Nature by Relying on the Great Elements (7):
First, the Earth Element.

"If one contemplates the nature of earth, it is characterized by solidity and obstruction rather than penetration; as a conditioned state, it is not the nature of the sages. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"

The Bodhisattva Earth-Holder, by means of his level mind-ground, perceived that internal and external objects fundamentally lack self-nature; they do not touch or rub against one another, for all are the Tathāgatagarbha.

Now, the nature of earth is characterized by solidity and obstruction; as a conditioned entity, its substance is not pervasive and it does not constitute the nature of a sage. Therefore, it is not the path of perfect penetration.
Second, the element of water:
"If one contemplates through the nature of water, mental conceptions are not real; suchness is beyond both thought and observation—how, then, could one attain perfect penetration?"

The youth Candraprabha, by practicing the contemplation of water, perceived that the water within his own body and the external fragrant water were of the same nature as true emptiness; they flowed as a single flavor, and he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Now, it is said that this contemplation is not separate from vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), saṃjñā (perception), and smṛti (mindfulness); how, then, could it be the true nature of suchness?
"Awakening and observation" (juéguān) are precisely vitarka and vicāra.
3. The Fire Element.

"If one contemplates through the nature of fire, one will grow weary of existence as not being true liberation; this is not the skillful means of the initial mind—how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"
The Vajra of Fire-Head contemplates the mind of excessive lust as it becomes the fire of wisdom; the body and mind experience a warm touch that flows unimpeded, giving rise to the great jewel-flame.
It is said here that because one generates renunciation through excessive lust, the contemplation is perfected as the fire of one's own nature.
This is merely a mind of aversion and seeking; how could it be called perfect illumination?
It is not the true gateway for transcending thought and is unsuitable for beginners; therefore, it must be excluded.
4. The Wind Element.
"If one contemplates through the nature of wind, motion and stillness are not without their opposites; yet opposites are not the Unsurpassed Awakening. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"

The Bodhisattva Vaidūryaprabha, by contemplating that the body, mind, and world are all moved by the power of delusory conditions—that the power of wind has no basis and is fundamentally non-existent—perceived immobility within movement and thereby realized the true mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Now, it is said that the nature of wind is movement; from movement arises stillness. Movement and stillness are relative; being relative, they are not true. How could this be the same as the perfect contemplation that enters the stream and causes objects to vanish?
5. The Great Element of Space:
"If one contemplates through the nature of emptiness, the dull and dark state was originally not awakening; since non-awakening differs from Bodhi, how could one attain perfect penetration?"

The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, by contemplating that the four great elements have no basis, that conceptual constructions arise and perish, and that space is non-dual and the Buddha-lands are fundamentally identical, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Now it is said that empty space is dark and obscured, produced by ignorance; it is not the luminosity of awakening, but differs from fundamental awakening, and therefore must be distinguished.
Sixth, the element of consciousness.
"If one observes by means of the nature of consciousness, observing that consciousness is not permanent, yet maintaining such a mind is itself a delusion; how then can one attain perfect penetration?

Maitreya Bodhisattva cultivated the contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), whereby he realized that throughout all the lands of the Tathāgatas—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—all are manifestations produced by the transformations of his own mind.

Now, it is said that the nature of consciousness arises and perishes from moment to moment, its攀緣 (pān-yuan, object-seeking) never ceasing; its substance is not permanent. If one merely eliminates the objects but does not eliminate the mind itself, one still falls into delusion—how could this be perfect penetration?
7. The Faculty of the Organs (*indriya*).

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; the nature of mindfulness is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. Cause and effect now manifest as distinct sensations; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"

"Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, by means of the *nien-fo* samādhi, completely gathered his six sense faculties; with pure mindfulness succeeding one another, he entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Now, it is said that all conditioned phenomena belong to the shifting and changing nature of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, and the very nature of mindfulness is subject to arising and ceasing, which is precisely impermanence. How can one obtain the fruit of permanence through a cause of impermanence? Therefore, this is not the perfect penetration."

Nevertheless, the method of Buddha-recollection is the most essential in this land; although it involves the cycle of arising and ceasing, by focusing one's thoughts with single-minded devotion and relying upon the power of the Buddha’s vows, one will be reborn in the Pure Land at dawn.
Once born in that land, one's progress becomes exceedingly swift, and the time for realization is imminent.

Here, the faculties of the various practitioners are revealed; since Avalokiteśvara is supreme, they must be distinguished according to the principle of elevating the superior and suppressing the inferior.
III. Verses on Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), in three parts:
A. Extensively revealing the gate of perfection, in four parts:
1. Designating and praising the Dharma entered.
"I now address the World-Honored One:

Since the Buddha has appeared in this Sahā world-system, the true essence of the teaching in this direction lies in purity within hearing and sound. If one wishes to attain samādhi, one must truly enter through hearing; thus one leaves suffering behind and attains liberation."
In the Sahā world, the faculty of hearing is the most acute; therefore, sound is employed as the Buddha-work.

Because consciousness arises from the auditory faculty to hear sounds, it induces the wisdom of hearing within the sixth consciousness, which takes names, phrases, and syllables as its objects. This perfumes the seeds of understanding in the mind, which are then received as the essence of the teaching; thus, it is said that the essence of the teaching resides in sound and hearing.
Once the essence of the teaching has been established, one then contemplates and practices it, entering samādhi and achieving great liberation.
Second, a brief praise of those capable of entering [this state].

"How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he has entered buddha-lands as minute as motes of dust, attaining the power of great mastery and bestowing fearlessness upon sentient beings."
"Wondrous Sound, Avalokiteśvara, Brahma-sound, Ocean-tide Sound; you bring peace and security to all who seek salvation in the world, and those who transcend the world attain the eternal abode.

The first line is a general title and praise; the next two lines praise the thirty-two manifestations; the following two lines praise the fourteen fearlessnesses along with the four inconceivables; and the final two lines praise his virtuous titles.
Sublime Sound (Ghoṣa) is the essence, while Avalokiteśvara is the function; these also represent the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional, as well as self-benefit and benefiting others.
"Brahma" (Brahman) carries the meaning of purity, which establishes the essence.
"The ocean tides must not miss their appointed time" explains the function [of the teaching].
The two lines following "saving the world" conclude with an exaltation of its benefits: first, one attains worldly peace and happiness; finally, one realizes ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
3. An Extensive Analysis of the Sense Organs of Perfect Penetration, in two parts:
1. Revealing the Nature of Hearing, in two parts:
1. A Comparative Analysis of the Real, in three parts:
First, the Perfect Reality:

"I now address the Tathāgata as Avalokiteśvara has taught: For example, when a person dwells in quietude and drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions, they hear them at once in all ten places; this is the Perfect Reality."
This is the virtue of liberation.

Just as the samādhis previously described by Avalokiteśvara, that which is attained therein is exceptionally sublime; its response to sentient beings is unfailing, reaching everywhere to provide appropriate transformation.
"The ten directions" refers to the ten realms.
"Beating the drum" refers to the activation of the spiritual capacity.
"Hearing it all at once" means that the response does not fail its timing.
This refers to the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya), which is immeasurable and nothing that is invoked fails to respond;
hence it is called "Perfect Reality. Second is "Pervasive Reality":
"The eyes do not perceive what is beyond obstructions; the same is true for the mouth and nose. The body only knows through contact; mental thoughts are chaotic and without order."
"Listening to sounds through a wall, one can hear them both from afar and nearby; since the five sense organs are not equal in this regard, this is the penetration of reality.
This is the virtue of Prajñā.

The first four phrases exclude what is not permeable; as for the last two phrases concerning the mouth and nose, the wording of the sūtra is inverted. Therefore, the examples—the mouth and nose—are presented first, followed by the subject of the analogy—the body faculty (*kāyendriya*). This was likely done by the translator to follow the sequence of the faculties more closely.
The four lines following "separated by a wall" precisely reveal that the ear-faculty differs from the preceding five; for this reason, it is named the "penetrating true ear.
Third, the "ever-true": two parts.
First, the precise revelation.

"The nature of sound consists of movement and stillness; within hearing, it appears as existence or non-existence. When there is no sound, it is called 'no-hearing,' yet this is not a true absence of the nature of hearing.
Since sound does not exist, there is no cessation; since sound exists, there is no birth. Being perfectly free from both birth and cessation, this is the eternal reality."
This is the virtue of the Dharma-body.
Within hearing itself, there is movement and stillness; these are spoken of as existence and non-existence, but this does not mean that the nature of hearing itself is existent or non-existent.

If worldly people were to call it "no-hearing" at the time when sound is not heard, then the nature of hearing would have already perished; yet when the dust of sound arises again, who is there to hear it?
Thus one knows that while sounds exist, the nature of hearing does not arise;
when sounds are absent, the nature of hearing does not perish.
Since it is entirely free from both arising and perishing, it is for this reason termed the eternally true reality.
2. Explanation and Confirmation:
"Even if one is in a dream, it is not non-existent due to a lack of thought; yet when awakening and contemplation transcend discursive thinking, body and mind can no longer reach it."

As before, when one is in deep sleep and mental activity does not function, hearing the sound of pounding rice, one perceives it as something else; at such a time, how could one be mindful of stillness or movement?
One should know that the nature of hearing is uninterrupted; therefore, it is said that it is not absent when one is not thinking.
Regarding "exiting from vitarka and vicāra through reflection": since this is not associated with mindfulness and conceptualization, it transcends the sphere of vitarka, vicāra, and reflection.
The translator’s rephrasing was incomplete, which resulted in the inversion of the phrasing.
Vitarka and vicāra are, respectively, *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
*Cintā* (reflection) is the universal mental factor (*sarvatraga-cetanā*).
Since both are mental concomitants (*caitta*) and are mutually non-associated (*asamprayukta*), they are termed "emergence" (*niṣkramaṇa*).
Furthermore, awakening is original awakening, which is precisely the nature of hearing.
Contemplation is illumination.
This follows the sequence of the text.
2. Distinguishing what is not [the truth] to reveal what is.

"Now, in this Sahā world, the treatises on sound and grammar are proclaimed and made clear; yet sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing, and thus they wander in transmigration by following after sounds."

"Even though Ānanda possesses a powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts; is this not because he follows where he sinks? By reversing the flow, one attains freedom from delusion.

The first two lines generally clarify that in this realm, one enters by means of vocal teaching; since sounds, names, phrases, and sentences can explain the meaning of the Dharma, sentient beings hear them and thereby achieve understanding—hence it is called "proclaiming and clarifying."

The next four lines correctly eliminate errors and misconceptions: if one merely follows the sounds of the teachings, one cannot transcend conditions to enter the stream and reflect back; this is precisely to be deluded regarding the fundamental nature of hearing and to follow after sounds instead.
Therefore, it is said that although Ānanda had attained great learning, he was unable to eliminate mental marks; he was turned by sounds and could not escape the delusions of arising and ceasing.

The latter two phrases conclude the refutation to reveal the truth: "revolving the flow" means returning the flow. This constitutes entering the stream and losing the object, wherein one perceives only the nature of hearing.
Since arising and ceasing have both ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one; therefore, it is called "non-delusion.
Second, the clarification of contemplative practice, in four parts: first, the address.
“Ānanda, listen attentively! Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic strength, I shall proclaim the Vajra King, the inconceivable, illusory-like, true samādhi of the Mother of Buddhas.”
As for "Vajra" and "like an illusion," these have already been explained above.
Because the Tathāgatas of the three periods transcend through a single gate, it is called the "Mother of Buddhas.
Furthermore, "Vajra" is emptiness.
"Like an illusion" refers to the provisional;
"Mother of Buddhas" refers to the middle.
Second, the refutation of errors.

"You have heard from as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust all the gates of secret mystery; yet, without first eliminating the outflows of desire, you harbor this learning and thereby commit an error.
You intend to maintain the Buddhas through hearing, so why do you not hear that which hears?"
Although one may uphold the treasury of the Dharma, if one cannot relinquish hearing to contemplate its own nature, one incurs error.

If one upholds the Buddha-dharma of others according to worldly characteristics of the śrāvakas, it is better to reflect back upon one's own faculty of hearing to realize the true samādhi; therefore, it is called "hearing-hearing."
III. The Correct Demonstration, in two parts:
A. The Correct Clarification of Contemplative Practice, in three parts:
1. The Dharma, in three parts:
First, the revolving of the faculties to escape from objects:
"Hearing does not arise spontaneously; it has a name because of sound. When the hearing revolves and detaches itself from sound, who could give a name to that which is capable of such detachment?"
"When one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation.
The "hearing" within seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing arises in accordance with sound; it is not the fundamental nature.
As stated above: "Just as you now listen to my Dharma, this is precisely the arising of discrimination based on sound," and so forth.

If one can abandon conditions to contemplate the nature, the characteristic of hearing will not arise; the objects of movement and stillness will vanish, and neither subject nor object will constrain it. Therefore, it is called liberation.
Since bondage cannot be attained, liberation likewise cannot be named.
As it is with one faculty, so it is with all six faculties.
Second, when objects dissolve, awareness manifests.

"Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the faculties are removed, the dust is extinguished and awareness becomes perfectly pure.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have become cataracts through delusion, and all phenomena within the three realms are but empty flowers.

The essence of seeing and hearing is empty and fundamentally unobtainable; furthermore, it is likened to an illusion. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The triple world is false and deceptive, produced solely by the mind."
The preceding passage states: "Because seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the conditions for illusory affliction, there exist the various impure lands of the ten directions.

When the cataract is removed and the flowers vanish, when hearing returns to its source and sensory objects dissolve, the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind becomes manifest, perfect, and pure; this is partial realization."
3. Awakening is ultimately unimpeded.
"Purity reaches its ultimate limit and luminosity penetrates through; in silent illumination, it encompasses the void. Returning to observe the world, it is like a matter within a dream."
"Even if Mātanga appears in a dream, who could detain your form?
"Ultimate purity" refers to the perfection of the liberation of full purity.
"Pervasive illumination" refers to the completion of the prajñā of full awakening.
Quiescent illumination refers to the ultimate state of the true reality of the Dharmakāya.

Once the three virtues are perfected and the three obstructions are forever exhausted, it is like awakening from a great dream or the blossoming of a lotus flower; looking back at the world, who could remain an obstacle?
This is the ultimate realization.
Second, the analogy:
"It is like a skillful worldly illusionist who conjures various men and women; although their various faculties appear to move, they are all pulled by a single mechanism."
"When the workings of the mind cease and one returns to stillness, all illusions become devoid of inherent nature.
The "illusionist" is the true nature (*tathatā*).
Because it possesses the meaning of following conditions (*pratyaya*), it is called "skillful."
Illusory phenomena are ignorance;
male and female are the six sense faculties.
A single stimulus is the illusory phenomenon; when the stimulus ceases, the illusion vanishes, delusion is extinguished, and the faculties return to their original state.
The illusionist is ignorance; the illusory phenomena are the mental consciousness.
The remaining correspondences are the same as previously assigned.
The man and woman created by illusion must have something upon which they depend; this is a metaphor for the true nature.
Third, the synthesis:
"The six sense organs are also like this: originally depending on a single brilliant clarity, they are divided into six harmonious combinations."
"In one place, rest and renewal are achieved; the six functions all fail to arise. The first phrase provides a general heading;
the second phrase corresponds to the illusionist; the third phrase corresponds to the man and woman; and the final two phrases correspond to the cessation of activity and so forth.
If the ignorance of the ear-faculty is destroyed, the other faculties are likewise destroyed; thus, none are established as real.
Second, the benefits of accomplishing this contemplation:

"Dust and defilements vanish at the mere thought [of it], and one achieves perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous clarity. While remaining dust-like, one is still among those in training; when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata."
"If even one faculty is restored, defilements will naturally vanish.
As stated in the preceding passage: 'Perceptual images are the dust, and cognitive consciousness is the grime; when both are removed, your Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright.'"
Therefore, it is said that "perfectly accomplished, luminous, pure, and wondrous.
This refers to the threefold merit (tridharmakāya) being perfectly manifested, neither vertical nor horizontal, nor sequential nor separate; thus, it is called "wondrous" (*miao*).

The latter two phrases conclude the stage: the former phrase indicates that the merit of cessation (*prahāṇa*) is not yet perfected, while the latter phrase indicates that the merit of wisdom (*jñāna*) is fully complete.
These can be understood through their mutual manifestation.
Fourth, the exhortation to practice:

"O Great Assembly and Ānanda, turn back the mechanism of your inverted hearing; by reversing the hearing to hear your own nature, that nature will achieve the Unsurpassed Way. Such is the reality of perfect penetration."
"Exhorting one to turn back from inverted hearing-faculties and instead contemplate the nature of hearing, when the nature of hearing is perfected, Bodhi may be hoped for.
The final phrase concludes by forming the seal."
4. Conclusion and Manifestation of Common Proof:
"This is the single path to nirvāṇa for countless buddhas.
All Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this path;"
The bodhisattvas of the present have each now entered perfect clarity;
those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this Dharma.
I, too, have realized it through this path, not only Avalokiteśvara.
The first two lines generally indicate that all Buddhas attain nirvana through this very gate.
The subsequent section, beginning with "In the past," specifically enumerates those of the three periods of time and cites Mañjuśrī as well, all serving as testimony for this same point.
2. Further Clarification on the Appropriate Differences.
"Truly as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has inquired of me regarding various skillful means to rescue those in the final kalpa who seek to transcend the world."
In achieving the mind of nirvana, Avalokiteśvara is supreme.

All other skillful means are the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha; by engaging with phenomena while relinquishing worldly toil, one does not rely on long-term cultivation and study, for both the shallow and the deep are taught through the same Dharma.

The first four lines of the verse are the Buddha’s instruction to discern [the practitioners]; the latter two lines directly point to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanmen), clearly showing it to be the most appropriate.

The remaining five lines clarify that the twenty-four sages each achieved their contemplative practice (*guanxing*) according to their respective causes and circumstances; these were all brought about by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*vīrya*) and skillful means (*upāya*) to enable them to attain the Way. This is not a dharma-gate for the simultaneous entry of both shallow and deep capacities through long-term cultivation and study.
This conversely reveals that Avalokiteśvara is a dharma-gate for both shallow and deep capacities to be taught together and enter together—a method for long-term cultivation and study.
Third, the conclusion of the vow and exhortation to study.

"I prostrate to the Tathāgatagarbha, untainted and inconceivable. I pray that you bestow your grace upon those of the future, so that they may have no doubt regarding this gateway; may it be easily accomplished through skillful means, such that it may be used to instruct Ānanda and those sinking in the delusions of the final age."
"Yet, by cultivating through this faculty alone, one attains perfect penetration that surpasses others; such is the true mind.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the single essence of the Triple Gem; it is the principle to be entered, for it is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature.

I pray that you will add the following five lines as the formal conclusion of the vow; however, the last two lines merely encourage study, while the final line is Mañjuśrī’s own selection of the perfect and penetrating mind, which is truly without falsehood because it is not constrained by personal sentiment.
3. The Assembly Attains Benefit.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly experienced a state of total clarity in body and mind, receiving a profound revelation.
They contemplated the Buddha’s Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa as being like a person who has traveled far away on business and, before returning, clearly understands the path leading back home.

The entire assembly—gods, dragons, and the eight classes of supernatural beings; those of the two vehicles still in training; and all the newly resolved bodhisattvas, numbering as many as ten Ganges-sands—all attained their original mind, became free from dust and defilement, and achieved the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Upon hearing these verses, the bhikṣuṇī Śīlā attained arhatship.
Immeasurable sentient beings all gave rise to the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is peerless.
The capacities of those in this single assembly vary; their levels differ, being both great and small.

When the preceding section on Avalokiteśvara was concluded, the Buddhas emitted light that came from one another to bestow empowerment, simultaneously empowering the great bodhisattvas and the arhats.
Those who receive that light simultaneously attain the Vajra Samādhi;
this reveals that the various distinct contemplation-gates of the twenty-four sages are all at once perfectly entered into the cultivation and realization of Avalokiteśvara.
Now, when Ānanda and the others who were beginners heard these verses, they each attained realization according to their respective stages.

While Ānanda and the others had just begun to realize perfect penetration by entering through the faculty of hearing, they had not yet attained full certification; therefore, it is said that they "clearly understood the path leading back to their own home."

Among those hosts of devas and nāgas, as well as those of small learning, ten times the number of Ganges sands attained the purity of the Dharma-eye from within the first ten stages of the Mahāyāna; they immediately entered the stage of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) of the First Ground (prathamabhūmi).
The bhikṣuṇī Śrī was one who had attained the third fruit; she has now become one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Those who had not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment were immeasurable in number; they all gave rise to the aspiration for the Way and immediately attained realization and understanding of the Mahāyāna.
Third, the practice of accomplishing the departure from demonic activities.

Although the preceding sections have extensively explained the complete realization through cultivation and verification, for ordinary beginners the obstacles and difficulties are particularly profound; how much more so in this final age when heterodox schools arise in chaotic competition, where perverse words delude the orthodox, demonic sophistry mimics the true, spurious accounts abound, and those who follow such currents are numerous.

If one does not discern and distinguish [the true from the false], it will hinder correct practice; therefore, one must verify [the practitioner] through the lens of precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, whereby the source of their deviation will naturally be revealed.
Thus, although all ninety-six types of non-Buddhist practitioners are capable of practicing dhyāna, they lack the virtue of the precepts.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If Māra can even transform himself into the form of a Buddha, how could he not delude the world by appearing as a Bodhisattva of the Four Reliances?
Therefore, the Buddha has extensively taught that if anyone says it is permissible to keep the eight impure things, this is the teaching of Māra."
"Even external objects are not permitted to be possessed, let alone the fundamental greed, anger, and delusion that underlie lust, theft, killing, and falsehood.

There are foolish people in the world who, deluded by Māra, slander the precepts, claiming they belong to the Hīnayāna, while they themselves profess to be Mahāyāna practitioners free from hindrances and constraints; this shall be extensively refuted later in the sutra."
All of these are the works of Māra; therefore, the Buddha strictly cautioned against them. This is called the definitive, clear teaching of the Mahāyāna.
Ānanda, possessing great transformative power, took pity on those of the future who would surely fall into the perils of Māra, and thus earnestly made this request as a perpetual and true admonition.
Section Two:
One, Ānanda’s inquiry during his contemplation, in three parts.
First, the narration of what he has realized.

Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage before the great assembly, and with a mind and conduct perfectly clear and bright, he was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy. Desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future, he prostrated himself and addressed the Buddha:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, I have now awakened to the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood; practicing within it, I have attained freedom from doubt."
"Perfect penetration is precisely the path traversed by the mind; hence it is called the 'traces of the mind.
Since my realization is profound, I am free from doubt;
yet, as many difficulties lie ahead, I wish to further elaborate upon this."
Regarding "sorrow and joy": one rejoices in what has now been realized and feels sorrow for those who will practice hereafter.
Second, the statement of one's vow:
"I have often heard the Tathāgata speak these words:"
"To cross others first before one has crossed oneself is the aspiration of a Bodhisattva.
To have perfected one's own awakening and then be able to awaken others is the manifestation of a Tathāgata in the world."
"Although I have not yet attained liberation myself, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final age.
There are two types of Bodhisattvas:

the first is those with superior wisdom, who first attain the fruit of Buddhahood and subsequently deliver sentient beings; [the second is those with superior merit, who first deliver sentient beings and subsequently attain the fruit of Buddhahood].

Second is the increase of compassion (*karuṇā*): because the mind’s urgency to deliver sentient beings is so intense, one intentionally retains afflictions (*kleśa*) to moisten rebirth within the three realms.
Now, to vow to deliver sentient beings while not yet having been delivered oneself is precisely the increase of compassion.
3. Stating the Request:
"World-Honored One!

These sentient beings are gradually moving further away from the Buddha, and false teachers preaching the Dharma are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. We wish to gather their minds and lead them into samādhi; how may we cause them to establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), remain far removed from demonic activities, and attain a state of non-retrogression regarding the mind of bodhi?"
"These sentient beings have inferior faculties; this is the inferiority of their roots.
They are gradually moving further away from the Buddha; this is the inferiority of the time.
Teachers of false doctrines abound; this is the abundance of difficulties."

In this degenerate age, understanding is clouded and delusive obstacles are particularly numerous; it is difficult to advance in the cultivation of meditative concentration and the gathering of the mind. How much more so when encountering demonic delusions and false views increasingly proliferate—how can one avoid regression in the practice and realization of the preparatory stages?
II. The Tathāgata’s Extensive Proclamation, in two parts: A.
Praising the Request and Granting Permission to Teach.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda amidst the great assembly:
"Excellent! Excellent!
Just as you have asked, one should establish the site of enlightenment to rescue and protect sentient beings drowning in the final age."
"Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly responded, "So be it," and respectfully received the instruction.

Regarding the ritual practice of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, one must cultivate both principle and phenomena: internally upholding the root of the precepts and externally relying on the mind-mantra; when the internal and external support each other, the power of the Way is easily accomplished.
I shall proclaim this for you; you should contemplate it well.
Second, the actual extensive exposition has two parts:
first, one’s own practice free from Māra; second...
I. General Explanation of the Three Trainings. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You have often heard me, within the Vinaya, proclaim the three principles of definitive practice: namely, taking the restraint of the mind as the precepts; from the precepts arises concentration; and from concentration issues forth wisdom. These are called the three trainings in the absence of outflows."
While various practices may differ according to the capacities of those to be trained, these three must necessarily be taught.
Furthermore, as they are the definitive causes for attaining Buddhahood—being the same for every Buddha—they are called the "Three Definitive Meanings."
2. A detailed exposition of the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).

Since the two gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) have already been discussed previously, this accords with the Vinaya and speaks of the eternal, being identical to *nirvāṇa*.
This section has four parts:
I. The Causes for Detachment from Desire, in two parts:
A. Correctly Distinguishing Right and Wrong, in three parts:
1. The Statement of the Subject.
“Ānanda! How does one collect the mind such that I call it ‘precept’?
If the minds of sentient beings within the six realms of all worlds are free from sexual desire, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.”
"Sensual desire is the root of birth and death; by reversing it, one's continuity ceases.
The *Awakening of Mahāyāna* states: 'All sentient beings correctly establish their nature and life because of sensual desire.'"
One should know that craving is the root of saṃsāra; because various desires assist in the arousal of the nature of craving, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.
II. The formal exposition has two parts:
first, citing faults to reveal what is incorrect; second... [the remainder of the text follows].
First, desire is the cause of Māra.
"If you practice samādhi with the intent to transcend worldly toil, yet do not eliminate the mind of lust, you cannot escape from the dust of the world;
even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into the path of Māra."

The high-grade were māra kings, the middle-grade were māra subjects, and the low-grade were māra women; these various māras also had their own followers, each of whom claimed to have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

When Māra practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without severing sensual desire, his concentration accords with his delusions and is easily accomplished; those whose practice is profound constitute the superior grade, while those whose practice is shallow constitute the middling and inferior grades.

Although they do not sever desire, they cultivate meditative concentration and merit; according to the superiority or inferiority of their merit, they form three grades. By the power of their false concentration, they obtain the five supernormal powers as a karmic retribution, and by means of their tainted merit, they are born into the realm of the celestial Māras.
Having attained a slight degree of meditative concentration, they fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, each claiming for themselves that they have realized the Unsurpassed Way.
Second, there will be much delusion in the future:

"After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such demonic followers will flourish in the world; they will widely practice greed and lust while posing as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), causing all sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and false views and lose the path to Bodhi."

Sentient beings in the final age lack the eye of the True Dharma and are frequently deluded by Māra; they extensively practice greed and lust, falsely claiming to be virtuous friends, seducing and leading the ignorant astray so that they lose the Right Path and encounter suffering. You should examine this deeply and not allow them to find an opportunity.
2. Conclusion and Exhortation:

"If you teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, they must first sever sexual desire in the mind; this is called the Tathāgata’s foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction from the Buddhas of the past."

Although these precepts share the same name as those of the Hīnayāna, their practice and observance differ; here, one guards every internal thought-moment, maintaining equanimity regarding both light and heavy offenses.
In that case, the matter is accomplished through conditions, and the gravity of the offense follows the specific precept.
Therefore, it is said: "First, one must sever sexual desire in the mind.
Thus, the Treatise says:
When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.
Therefore, this is entirely distinct from the observance of precepts in the Lesser Vehicle.
Third, the exhortation and admonition, in two parts:
First, reiterating the faults and afflictions, in two parts:
first, manifesting through a simile: "Therefore, Ānanda!"

If one does not sever lust yet cultivates meditative concentration, it is like steaming sand and gravel in the hope of producing rice; even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it will still be called nothing but hot sand. Why is this?
"This is not the essence of rice, for it is composed of sand and gravel.

Likewise, the dharmas of precept, concentration, and wisdom can give rise to the Dharma-body; yet if the root of the precepts is incomplete, how can one cultivate meditation and wisdom in vain? How could a pure and wondrous body ever be born from lustful desire?
The causes for [rebirth as] sand or rice are distinct; who could calculate their kalpas?
Second, the summary of the faults:

"If you seek the Buddha’s wondrous fruit with a lustful body, even if you attain wondrous enlightenment, it will all be rooted in lust. With lust at its very foundation, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape them. By what path can you cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata?"
Without precepts there is no meditation; without meditation there is no wisdom.
If the root of the precepts is not pure, how can the meditation and wisdom one practices become pure?
Because they are impure, though they exist, they are as if non-existent.
If precepts, concentration, and wisdom are lost, one will naturally revolve in saṃsāra; this ultimately cannot be the fruit of sagehood.
Second, the exhortation to sever [the defilements]:
"One must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind, such that even the nature of 'severing' is non-existent; only then can one hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha."
A person who truly upholds the precepts does not even maintain the appearance of upholding them; how much less would they allow their body or mind to transgress the grave prohibitions?

As the subsequent text states: "Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth are termed the realm of ghosts; their absence is termed the heavenly realm. When both existence and non-existence are absent, and even this 'absence of duality' is extinguished, this is called the wondrously arising *samādhi*."
2. Conclusion on the Right and the Wrong:
"What I have spoken thus is called the teaching of the Buddha; what is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyas.
[The correct transcription is] Pāpīya, which means "the Evil One" (Māra).
Pāpīyān is a corruption [of the name].
Second, abandoning the causes of killing, which has two parts:
first, correctly distinguishing right from wrong, which has three sections:
1. The Indication: "Ānanda!
Furthermore, if the beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor a mind of killing, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death."
"Killing one another and seeking retribution, their bonds and calamities become entangled; if one were to simply stop them, they would not continue.
The rest is as in the text.
II. The Main Exposition has two parts:
First, pointing out faults to reveal what is not [the Way], in two parts:
First, killing as a cause for becoming a ghost.
"You cultivate samādhi, fundamentally seeking to emerge from worldly toil; yet if the mind of killing is not eliminated, you cannot emerge from the dust."
Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not cease killing, they will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits.
Those of the highest grade become great ghosts; those of the middle grade become flying yakṣas, various ghost generals, and the like; those of the lowest grade shall become earth-walking rākṣasas.
Those various ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
By practicing dhyāna while maintaining a murderous intent, one is reborn as a spirit;
through deep merit and abundant blessings, one becomes a powerful ghost, such as those enshrined in sacrifices at the Five Peaks and the Four Rivers.

Those of shallow merit and inferior fortune are ranked among the middle and lower classes; they are governed by the eight classes of beings and include the rākṣasa nations along the shores of the great ocean.
Because they have practiced meditative concentration, they all possess karmic supernormal powers that are swift and unimpeded.
Because they do not cease from killing, they undergo this miserable rebirth and are driven into service for the gods.
If one does not cultivate meditative concentration nor cultivate merit, but practices only slaughter, one enters directly into hell without such gradations of mitigation.
2. Many delusions in the future, in three parts:
first, the explicit explanation.
"After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, claiming that by eating meat one attains the path to Bodhi."
"Killing living beings and eating their flesh is an act that creates enmity with sentient beings; how can one fail to sever this and attain the path to Bodhi?
Second, the distinction: 'Ānanda!'"
"I have permitted the bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat; these meats are all produced through my supernatural power and originally possess no life-force.
You, O Brahmin, live in a land that is largely damp and humid, further compounded by sand and gravel, such that grasses and vegetables do not grow."
It is through the empowerment of my great compassionate supernatural power that, by virtue of great kindness and compassion, [the meat] is provisionally named "flesh," and you obtain its flavor.
How can it be that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who eat the flesh of sentient beings still call themselves disciples of Śākya?
In the fourth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Kāśyapa asks:
"Why did the Tathāgata previously permit bhikṣus to eat the three kinds of pure meat?
The Buddha replied:
"It is merely because they were gradually established according to specific circumstances.

Furthermore, there are seven kinds and nine kinds; that we now speak of five is due to the increase or decrease found in various sutras, with the numbers being assigned according to one's own judgment.
The Buddha, through skillful means, provisionally permitted them to eat meat; this was not the ultimate teaching.
Third, he demonstrated the faults:

"You should know that even if these meat-eaters attain an opening of the mind that resembles samādhi, they are all great rākṣasas. When their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death; they are not disciples of the Buddha."
If such people continue to kill, devour, and eat one another without ceasing, how can they escape the three realms?
That which resembles *samādhi* is the concentration of ghosts and spirits.
It can also enable one to know the events of the past and future, resembling a state of wholesome concentration, as described in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Second, the conclusion and the clear admonition:

"When you teach the people of the world to practice samādhi, they must first cease killing; this is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past."
III. Admonition and Exhortation, in two parts: A.
Reiterating the Faults and Sufferings, in two parts: 1.
Explaining the Faults of Speech in Accordance with the Teaching; 2. [The second part].
First, the illustration by analogy: "Therefore, Ānanda!
If one does not cease killing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person who blocks his own ears and shouts at the top of his voice, seeking for others not to hear him."
"These are what are called 'seeking to hide what is manifest.
To practice dhyāna while stuffing one's ears, yet to commit murder with a loud voice—seeking a path that is not heard while flaunting manifest suffering—is this not tragic?"
2. The Analogy: "Pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas, when walking along a forked path, do not even tread upon living grass, let alone pull it up with their hands.
How could those of great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food?"
"Not treading on living grass" is not merely to avoid criticism; it is also a profound expression of compassionate mindfulness.
If one does not even step upon grass, how much less would one harm a living being?
Second, the reversal that reveals faults of the body has two parts:
First, the explicit clarification of what is to be avoided:
"If the bhikṣus do not wear silks, cottons, or floss-silk from the East, nor the boots, leather shoes, furs, or woolens of this land, nor milk, curd, or clarified butter."
In this way, a bhikṣu is truly liberated from the world; he has repaid his karmic debts from the past and no longer wanders within the three realms.

Since silk, cotton, furs, and wool are parts of sentient beings' bodies, and such a person does not wear them—being one who is truly liberated because they have repaid their karmic debts by no longer wandering within the three realms.

Second, the reason for the parable: "For what reason?"
"Adhering to their respective portions constitutes the condition for them.
It is like a person who eats the various grains from the earth; their feet do not leave the ground.
Adhering to the portion of sentient beings constitutes the condition for sentient beings.
If even those who abstain from grain in pursuit of ascension fail to reach their goal, how much less can eating or wearing [certain substances] lead to liberation?
Second, the exhortation to sever [these attachments]:

"I declare that person to be truly liberated whose body and mind, toward all sentient beings—whether in relation to the whole body or its parts—neither consume nor ingest anything through either the physical or mental channels."
"When the mind is free from greedy deliberation and the body does not engage in [unwholesome] conduct, and the nature of contrivance has utterly perished, one is naturally and truly liberated.
Second, the conclusion regarding the heterodox and the orthodox:
"What I have spoken in this way is called the Buddha’s teaching; what is not spoken in this way is the teaching of Pāpīyas."
III. Abandoning the Causes of Stealing, in two parts:
A. Correctly Distinguishing Right from Wrong, in three parts: 1. The Indication.
“Ānanda! Furthermore, if the minds of sentient beings within the six realms of the world do not steal, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death.
To take what is not given is an offense the very moment the thought arises; therefore, it is said that their minds do not steal.”
Second, the formal exposition, in three parts:
First, the exposition of its wrong practice, in two parts:
First, theft as the cause of wrong practice.
"As you cultivate samādhi, its very purpose is to emerge from worldly toil; yet if you do not eliminate the thieving mind, you cannot escape the dust of the world.

There are those of superior grade who are refined spirits, those of middling grade who are demonic enchanters, and those of inferior grade who are wicked men possessed by various demons.

"Though meditative concentration and wisdom may manifest, if greed and theft are not eliminated, even if one abandons lust and killing, one will still fall into deviant paths.

Spirits, demons, and various heterodox persons can all delude and confuse people, causing the masses to submit to them; they do not spare their own food or clothing, providing for others until their lives are exhausted."
If one does not cultivate dhyāna, one will go directly to hell.

"After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, such demonic and heterodox beings will flourish in the world; they will secretly harbor deceit and fraudulence while claiming to be 'good spiritual friends' (kalyāṇamitra).
