First, the clarification of right practice:
"I instruct the bhikṣus to wander for alms according to their direction, causing them to abandon greed and accomplish the path to Bodhi.

These bhikṣus do not cook food for themselves; they entrust their remaining lives to it, lodging as travelers within the Triple Realm, demonstrating a single journey and return, after which there is no coming back."

The bhikṣu begs for alms according to the Dharma and does not cook food himself, in order to abandon the fault of greed, to cultivate deep weariness toward his own arising, and to have no attachment to the triple world, like a traveler who merely passes through on his way.
2. Refuting Deviant Practices:

"How is it that these thieves, donning my robes, peddle the teachings of the Tathāgata for profit and engage in all manner of karmic deeds, all claiming them to be the Buddha-dharma, while they instead denigrate the bhikṣus who have left home and observed the precepts as followers of the Hīnayāna path?"
"Because of this, they mislead and delude immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell.

Though their bodies have left the household life, their minds do not enter the Way; they falsely wear the robes to create a semblance of appearance and trade upon the Tathāgata to create karma. On the contrary, they disparage those who possess the full precepts as mere provisional or inferior practitioners, while ostentatiously manifesting extraordinary deportment as the ultimate state. Thus they deceive and delude the ignorant, leading them into endless evil."

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Perversity," states: "After my parinirvāṇa, this Māra Pāpīyān will gradually corrupt and disrupt my True Dharma. He will even assume the forms of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and arhats, and with his outflowing body, he will claim it to be without outflows, thereby destroying my True Dharma. He will even say:

'There are no dharmas such as the four pārājikas, saṃghāvaśeṣas, aniyatas, naiḥsargika-pāyattikas, pratideśanīyas, śaikṣas, or adhikaraṇa-śamathas; nor are there the offenses of stealing, the five ānantaryas, or the icchantika. Even if one commits such offenses, there is no retribution.'"
Those who speak thus are all speaking the words of Māra; within my Buddha-dharma, those who commit such offenses as these should be severely disciplined.
If one does not uphold the precepts, how could they ever perceive the Buddha-nature?
2. A detailed exposition of the transformation of karma has two parts:
first, the actual presentation of the method.

"If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind to cultivate samādhi, he may before an image of the Tathāgata light a single lamp with his own body, burn a finger-joint, or apply a single stick of incense to his body."
I say that such a person has repaid all karmic debts from beginningless time at once; they bid a long farewell to the world and are forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*).
Although they have not yet clearly realized the path to supreme enlightenment, their mind is already resolved regarding the Dharma.
The acts of killing and stealing persist as opposing forces that do not vanish; they serve as conditions for the three realms and obstruct the path to Bodhi.

However, since the physical body can repay these causes, once the karmic debts from past lives are eliminated, one is forever liberated from the world; hence it is said that one takes a long farewell.
2. Conclusion on Requital:

"If I had not performed this minor cause of sacrificing my body, even though I have attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), I would inevitably have been reborn as a human being to repay my past debts, just as in the case of my [eating] horse-barley, exactly and without difference."
Previously it was said: "Mātanga is but a dream; who can retain your physical form? Now it is said:

"Even if you attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), you must surely repay your past debts. This demonstrates that karmic retribution does not perish; even after attaining the unconditioned, one still possesses a conditioned body in the present world and must still settle old debts.
How much more so, when one has not yet entirely escaped the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how could one hope to falsely evade the fruits of karma?
The citation of scriptural evidence regarding the retribution for karma is as explained elsewhere.
Third, the conclusion that establishes the clear admonition.

"If you teach the people of the world to practice samādhi and subsequently renounce theft, this is called the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas of the past."
3. Admonition and Exhortation, in two parts:
1. Illustrating non-interruption through a metaphor. "Therefore, Ānanda!..."

If one does not cease stealing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person pouring water into a leaking chalice; though they seek to fill it, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it will never be replenished.
To pour the water of meditative concentration into a chalice of broken precepts while seeking the fruit of fulfillment—this has been unbalanced for aeons of dust.
Whose fault is this? Is it not a matter of failing to exercise caution?

This means that while their internal virtue lacks substance, their external appearance deceives people; the vessel of their precepts has already been pierced, and much of the wholesome Dharma leaks away.
Second, he exhorts them to eliminate and sever [such faults].

“If there are bhikṣus who do not store even a fraction of what remains from their robes and alms bowls; who give the remnants of their begged food to hungry sentient beings; who join their palms in homage to the assembly at great gatherings; who regard being struck or reviled by others as equivalent to receiving praise; who ensure that both body and mind are completely relinquished; who share their own flesh, bones, and blood with all sentient beings; and who do not take the Buddha’s teachings of provisional meaning and twist them into their own interpretations to mislead beginners—the Buddha certifies such persons as having attained true samādhi.”
This passage exhorts one to abandon the four faults—namely, greed, pride, anger, and delusion—which can be seen by correlating them with the text.
Since the mind does not give rise to anger and the body does not inflict retaliation, it is said that "both are relinquished."

Because one regards all sentient beings and one’s own body as equal and non-dual, the body and mind do not harbor resentment; therefore, it is said that [the merit] is shared with sentient beings. Regarding those who take this provisional teaching (*neyārtha*) as their own understanding:

they do not turn the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*) into a method for solitary awakening within their own minds, using it instead to deceive ignorant beginners. This passage also proves that while within the provisional teachings one may obtain pure meat, in the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) everything is prohibited; one must not cling to the provisional teachings as being the ultimate teaching. To cling to the expedient and slander the real is also of this nature.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Foolish ordinary beings, consumed by evil views and deluded by perversity and intoxication, falsely claim that these are the teachings spoken by the Omniscient One.
Master Huī’s commentary explains:
"Those without wisdom do not understand that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is a skillful means; instead, they falsely claim it to be the ultimate teaching of an omniscient person."
2. Conclusion on the Deviant and the Correct:
"That which I have spoken is called the Buddha’s teaching; that which is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
4. Departing from False Causes, in two parts:
I. Correctly Distinguishing Right from Wrong, in three parts: A. The Indication. "Ānanda!..."

Thus, among the sentient beings of the six realms in this world, even if their bodies and minds are free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—such that these three practices are already perfected—if they engage in great falsehood, their *samādhi* will not attain purity; they will become demons of craving and views, losing the seed of the Tathāgata.
The causes of false speech arise from greed, delusion, and pride; if these are not severed, they result in craving and views.
Second, the formal analysis has two parts:
first, falsehood as the cause of suffering, which has two sub-parts: [1a]...
I. A Comparative Analysis, in two parts:
A. Exposing Fabrications, in two parts:
1. Setting forth the deception by means of a heading and enumeration.
"Those who have not attained claim to have attained; those who have not realized claim to have realized; or, seeking to be honored as the most supreme in the world, they say to others:

'I have now already attained the fruit of a Srotāpanna, the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an Anāgāmin, the path of an Arhat, the vehicle of a Pratyekabuddha, or the various stages of the Bodhisattvas from the ten bhūmis down to the stages prior to the bhūmis.'"
"He seeks their prostrations and repentance, coveting their offerings.
With a mind of ignorance and folly, he gives rise to great arrogance; because he seeks preeminence and craves those offerings, this delusion of craving and views is both powerful and rampant.

Because they give rise to false speech by claiming to have attained the fruits of realization of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles—when even speaking of having actually attained the fruits of the Path is not permitted, how much more so to speak falsely of what one has not attained?
2. Conclusion on the Invitation of Suffering.

"This icchantika extinguishes the seed of the Buddha; it is like a person cutting down a tāla tree with a sword. The Buddha has prophesied that this person’s roots of goodness are forever destroyed, that they shall have no further knowledge or vision, and that they will sink into the ocean of the three sufferings, never attaining samādhi."
The *icchantika* is one who has severed their roots of goodness; a great falsehood is equal to this transgression.
The "Chapter on the Perversions" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If someone should say:"
"I have already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
Because all possess Buddha-nature; those who possess Buddha-nature will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"You should know that such a person commits a pārājika offense. Why is this?
Although they possess the Buddha-nature, because they have not yet cultivated the various skillful means of goodness, they do not see it."
"Because they do not see [the truth], they cannot achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Thus we know that those who, without practicing even a slight degree of abandonment (*prahāṇa*), claim to be Buddhas, are all uttering great falsehoods; they commit a *pārājika* offense and are not disciples of the Buddha.
II. Clarifying the True and the Manifested, in two parts:
A. Listing the Manifested Deeds:

"After my parinirvāṇa, I shall command the various Bodhisattvas and Arhats to manifest their response-bodies (nirmāṇakāya) within that age of the Final Dharma; assuming various forms, they shall deliver those wandering in the cycle of rebirth."

Whether appearing as śramaṇas, lay householders, kings, ministers, or boys and girls—even as prostitutes, widows, thieves, or butchers—he associates with them as colleagues, praising the Buddha Vehicle and causing their bodies and minds to enter samādhi.
"By means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they benefit sentient beings through various forms of transformation.

Initially, they bring others onto the same path; subsequently, they encourage them toward the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). All of this is for the sake of benefiting others, not out of greed for personal gain."
2. The Admonition on Explicit Words:

"One must never say of oneself, 'I am a true Bodhisattva' or 'I am a true Arhat. To divulge the Buddha’s secret causes and speak lightly of one's junior studies is forbidden, except at the moment of death when there may be a final entrustment made in private."
"The true sages who benefit sentient beings are ultimately unfathomable; adhering to the Buddha’s regulations, they do not recklessly divulge [these matters].
This sacred and true cause is realized only by the sages themselves, and is therefore called the 'Secret Cause' (mi-yin); it must not be lightly spoken before those who have not yet studied."
Regarding "having entrusted something in secret," this does not refer to what is manifest.
It opens up the possibility of making a secret indication at the time of death to instruct a disciple, such as the incident of Guṇabhadra counting his fingers.
2. Conclusion and Reprimand:
"How can such a person delude sentient beings and commit a great falsehood?
2. Conclusion and Clear Admonition.

“If you teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, and subsequently eliminate all great false claims, this is called the Fourth Decisive, Pure, and Clear Instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One of the Buddhas of the Past.”
3. Admonition and Exhortation, in four parts:
first, illustrating that [the lineage] shall not be interrupted: "Therefore, Ānanda!..."
"If one does not abandon such great falsehood, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood; to seek its fragrance is impossible.
One carves the excrement of a person who utters falsehoods into the shape of the sandalwood of meditative concentration.
From afar they appear pleasing to the mind, but when approached closely, they emit a foul odor; those who seek the fragrance of the Way will never find it here.
Second, to illustrate the prevention of subtle transgressions:

"I teach that bhikṣus are the very site of the Way through their upright minds; even in all their actions throughout the four modes of deportment, they must be free from falsehood. How then can you claim for yourselves the dharmas of a superior man?"
The realization attained by those of the three vehicles constitutes the "superior human state" (*uttara-manuṣya-dharma*).
This passage uses the shallow to illustrate the profound: if even minor false speech is not permitted, how much more so great falsehood?
Third, the grave error illustrated by a further analogy:
"Suppose a destitute man falsely claims to be an emperor; he brings about his own execution and destruction. How much more so for a Dharma King—how could one falsely usurp such a title?"
"If the ground is not upright, the fruit will be crooked; seeking the Bodhi of the Buddha is like a person trying to bite their own navel—who can achieve anything?

The first metaphor illustrates that great falsehood ceases to be the root of suffering; the latter metaphor illustrates that seeking the Way ultimately lacks the principle of attainment, just as a person biting their navel can never reach it.
The *Chunqiu Zhuan* says: "If you do not plan ahead, later the ruler will find himself biting his own navel.
Fourth, the section on severing what cannot be remedied:
"If the minds of the bhikṣus are as straight as a bowstring and all things are true, they will enter samādhi forever free from demonic interference."
"I certify that this person shall achieve the unsurpassed enlightenment of a bodhisattva.
At all times, there is no falsehood whatsoever; if such a person as this truly seeks the Way, how could they not arrive swiftly!

If one displays external signs and physical forms, falsely claiming to have attained the Way, harboring flattery and crookedness within while scheming for fame and reputation without—how can this be called spiritual cultivation?

Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "In the defiled age, there are evil bhikṣus whose perverse wisdom and minds are flatteringly crooked; they claim to have attained what they have not attained, their hearts filled with arrogance. Even those who wear patched robes in secluded places, falsely calling themselves forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*), you should know that all such as these practice the works of Māra."
